channel: Private alpha · fresh start release candidate
title: TurboPanel Fresh Start
body: One new folder layout on every server, one fresh database baseline, folder names you choose once and keep, certificate authority rotations that finish on their own, and alerts for folders and certificates that need attention. This release needs a wipe: it cannot be installed over an earlier one.

sections.heading: This Release Needs a Wipe
items: Reset the panel database and every server, then install fresh. Do not update an existing panel or server to this release; it will refuse to start on an old database.

Why the folder layout cannot be moved in place: sites, apps and volumes now live in a different tree, and no old path is kept as a fallback. Carrying both would mean two sets of rules for who owns and can reach each folder.
Why the database starts again: every earlier change to the database is folded into one fresh baseline, with tables renamed and reshaped for launch. Nothing converts an older database to it.
Why servers are reset too: a Hosting Account, its folders and the panel's records of them must agree from the first day, and an older server's leftovers would break that.
This is the one reset. From this release on, every change to the database is a forward-only upgrade from the previous release, with a backup taken first.

sections.heading: Where Your Files Live
items: Each Hosting Account now has one tree under /srv/users/{owner}/. Inside it, every environment gets its own folder, and its sites and apps sit under services and its volumes under volumes: /srv/users/{owner}/{scope}/services and /srv/users/{owner}/{scope}/volumes.

The scope is the environment name. A service or volume can instead be placed in a shared scope called common, so every environment of that Hosting Account can use it. The choice is made when you create it and cannot be changed later.
Sites, apps and volumes are served from this tree, backups read a volume copy straight from its folder, and a deploy sends the folder of every service that runs on the host.

Deleting a volume asks the host to remove its folder, and you confirm the removal. Removing a service keeps its files. A container that runs as a user other than the Hosting Account's gets access set up for it when it is declared.

sections.heading: Folder Names and Locks
items: Folder names for services and volumes are short lowercase names, chosen when you create them. An organization can require readable names, require generated ones, or allow both.

Names are locked once something exists on a server, so a folder is never moved by accident: a service's folder name, the place (environment or common) it was created in, an environment's name while it has folders, and the project's short name once any folder exists.
A refused change says which folders are holding the lock, and a folder waiting for an offline server to remove it is named as the reason.
The Folders screen lists the folders that need attention, and lets you remove them or try again.

sections.heading: One Fresh Database Baseline
items: The panel's database history is now a single baseline instead of forty steps.
Table names are all one plain word. For example, the two-factor table is now totp and the grant table is now permission.
Database logins and the databases themselves have their own tables, a database login's rights are stored as real columns, and audit history and commands are stored by month.

sections.heading: Certificates
items: Rotating an organization's certificate authority now finishes on its own. Leaf certificates that were issued under the old authority and left behind are renewed instead of staying stuck, and the ones a rotation leaves behind are listed with an owner for each.

Alerts: a folder left behind on a server with nothing in the panel pointing to it, and a certificate that fails to renew, now raise an alert. The notification rules screen gives each alert a plain name.

sections.heading: Hosting and Environments
items: Domains is now called Hosting.

The environment's configuration page shows its hostnames, waits for them to load before it says there are none, and asks for a certificate when you save a web hostname. The certificate box appears only for web routes.

sections.heading: Safer Defaults
items: The SFTP jail, which locks files-only users into their own home, is now on by default for a new server. An explicit off is remembered and always wins, and a layout problem keeps it off with a message naming the Hosting Account.

A Postgres read/write login can no longer empty a table (TRUNCATE) or point a foreign key at one (REFERENCES), matching MySQL and MariaDB. Only the migration login can; an app that empties tables in its tests needs it.
The audit trail keeps 13 months. Older entries are removed in small batches, and a superadmin can change the window or keep everything.

sections.heading: Installing and Updating
items: The installer log is calmer and consistent from one step to the next.
The update bar says in plain words what it updates, calls the part you are looking at the web interface, and warns that the page may briefly show the updating screen.
After a deploy starts a site's web server, the deploy waits for it to come up before it calls the deploy failed.

title: TurboPanel 0.2.x
body: A new project and environment editor in the web app, a deploy you can cancel, certificates in one click, more ways to serve a site (four web engines and three PHP modes), a much tighter separation between site owners on a server, and a firewall you can preview before anything is applied.

sections.heading: The project and environment editor
items: Projects home: one card per project, the projects you opened recently, and deploys in progress.
A project has Environments, Base and Settings tabs. An environment has Overview, Deployments, Configuration and Settings tabs under one header.

The Base is the compose document that environments share. The Environments tab shows it first, then one card per environment: what is running now, the last deploy, a small map, the git branch, the server, and whether it "Follows the Base" with a number of changes or "Stands alone". New environment starts from the Base or from nothing and asks for a server.
Environment Overview draws the map of the environment, lists its services and latest deploys, and shows the "Changes from Base" card. The map is in the web app; the phone keeps its earlier Overview.

Configuration shows what an environment really runs, with a switch for only the changes from the Base, and lets you edit and save. The merged result is checked before it is saved, so a change that could not deploy is refused up front. The Base tab edits the shared compose document.
New Navy and Paper looks in the web app, with a Light, Dark or Match switcher.

sections.heading: Deploying and running
items: Cancel a deploy that is queued or running. It stops every server of that deploy, including servers still waiting their turn; once a deploy has switched over it can no longer be cancelled.
A failed deploy or command shows the line that says why, including which step of a server setup failed.

The control plane now records one run state per service (starting, running, unhealthy, crashing or stopped) and serves it through the API. The web Overview shows an app that is failing, with a Crash sheet and a Retry button, and a service that keeps crashing is stopped after 10 restarts in a row. Crash alerts are not part of this release.

A new environment deploys one step at a time: stop the old version, start the new one, wait for every service to be healthy, and roll back on its own if it is not. Deployment history says Sequential or In place, and Rolled back or Needs attention when a deploy did not finish. The strategy and the number of servers updated at once are set through the API; there is no screen for them yet.
Each environment picks its git branch, a push deploys the environments that build that branch, and history shows which push started a deploy.

A Node app receives the variables you set on it in its running process, and the app lists where each variable comes from. Node 26 is offered, and pnpm comes with every Node series. Secret site variables are sent to the server sealed.
WordPress sites are recognised and tagged, and the app warns when their database cannot work. Deleting an environment that has services asks you to stop it first and names what will go.

Every environment is its own Docker Compose project, so two environments cannot trip over each other on one server. Server status data carries a release link check from each server; there is no screen for it yet.

sections.heading: Domains and certificates
items: One-click Let's Encrypt for each domain. The app checks DNS first and shows the certificate state (Test certificate, Waiting for DNS, Getting a certificate, Secure, Renewal failed); the expiry date is recorded from the server.
"Also redirect www to this domain" serves the www name as a permanent redirect.
The Hosting tab lets you pick a hostname and shows only that hostname's settings.
New organization certificate authorities use P-384 keys and last 15 years.

sections.heading: Sites, web engines and PHP
items: Sites can be served by Caddy, nginx, Apache or OpenLiteSpeed, or by nginx in front of Apache.
PHP runs in one of three modes: FastCGI (the default), php-fpm, or OpenLiteSpeed's lsphp as a process of its own. Every site's PHP runs as the site owner's Linux user, with its own memory limit.

An organization owner or manager chooses which PHP modes the organization offers and can narrow that for each server. A site picks its mode in the visual editor or in its compose document; a mode the policy does not allow stops the deploy with a clear message.

Remote build sources (building from an address on the internet) are off until the organization allows them, and risky build options in a compose document are refused unless the organization allows them.
A site owner's Linux user can be named in plain, partial or random form, with an organization default that can be locked.

sections.heading: Keeping site owners apart
items: Root owns a site owner's home folder and the folders that hold published releases. The owner writes only to their own folders (home, data, tmp, and each site's webroot and shared folders), so a release cannot be changed after it is published.
Native and static builds run in a sandbox as an unprivileged build user with public internet access only, 4 GB of memory, 2 CPUs and 30 minutes, one build at a time per server.

SSH keys are managed by the app and keys placed in a home folder are ignored; port forwarding is off. Files-only owners are locked into their own home with an SFTP jail, which a new server switches on by itself.
The web servers run as their own unprivileged accounts, and a link inside one site is followed only when its owner matches the file it points to.
The Docker gate is installed wherever Docker runs on a managed server. It is in observe mode: it records what it would refuse and only turns away malformed requests.

sections.heading: Firewall
items: Firewall pages for the organization policy, your own rules, and each server's mode and preview. Nothing is applied to a server unless an operator opts that one server in.
When a firewall is applied, a safety net rolls it back unless the server confirms it still works, and it is restored after a reboot. Saving an SSH list that leaves you out asks you to confirm first.

sections.heading: Databases, storage and backups
items: Scheduled and on-demand backups for storage copies, with restore and delete from the app, and a schedules panel for managed databases of all three engines.
A managed Postgres can fail over to a failover replica on its own when the primary is found dead; recoveries no longer leave a cluster stuck.

MySQL and MariaDB logins now do the three jobs their names say. A read/write login can change data but can no longer create, change or drop tables, indexes, views, routines, triggers or events; the migration login can do all of that inside its own database, and only the Database admin login can hand rights to others. Every existing read/write login is tightened at the next apply of its cluster, with no grace period. Before you update, check that no app runs its migrations as a read/write login, and move any that does to a migration login first. TurboPanel refuses to create a read/write login, or change one to read/write, on a server whose daemon is out of date, until it is updated.

When you create a database login you pick one of three jobs in the app: read-only, read/write or migration. There is also a Database admin login for each cluster, and every login can be limited to the places it may connect from and to a number of connections. Review the limits on logins that are reachable from outside the server.
The root database login now works only from the server itself, its containers and the panel servers. If anything outside those connects as root, give it its own login instead.

Every new Postgres database gets a no-login owner role, and you can choose which login owns the database. Creating a database without an owner role, or with a name longer than 54 characters, is refused.

MySQL and MariaDB database names that contain an underscore are now granted by exact name: a grant on wp_site no longer also matches wpXsite. Older broad grants are removed at the next apply, so a login that quietly relied on a look-alike name loses that access; check the logins of any database with an underscore in its name.
"What can this login do?" shows the permissions a database login really has on the server, so you can check a login against what you meant to give it.

sections.heading: Organizations, people and notifications
items: The Activity page lists deploy work across the whole organization, running and recently failed.

A Members screen with Remove and Leave, a Change password screen with a breached-password check, and an organization setting that asks people to confirm it is them before permanent actions (off by default).

Email notification channels confirm their address from an emailed link, and every channel can use a digest and quiet hours. A critical event is never held back by either. Failed emails are retried later and then set aside.
Plain-language reasons for failed updates, billing refusals and other errors across the app.

sections.heading: Updates and billing
items: Updates name the version and the piece being updated, show a calm reconnecting state while the control plane restarts, and update one server at a time by default; an environment can start more at once. A server already on the target build no longer shows a stale update error.

The capacity pages say server limit. A server limit change checks its proration date first, spare larger server slots follow the recommended size, a refusal to remove a license says how many are in use, and a past-due subscription ends on Stripe's own retry schedule.
A fresh install now runs its steps in the right order, and an update restarts the panel so the new version is the one running. Update the servers' daemons before or together with the panel.

sections.heading: Reliability and safety
items: Many reliability and safety improvements to builds, hosting, sign-in, notifications and updates across the control plane, daemon and web app, with no change to how you use them.

title: TurboPanel 0.1.0
body: The first packaged release. Self-hosted installs from a single command (curl -fsSL turbopanel.sh | sh) that pulls signed-off packages from GitHub Releases, verifies each against its manifest, converges the host and hands off to the install wizard; the same command with a license enrols a server. Sign in with a passkey or TOTP second factor, or with GitHub or Google; invite teammates by email with a capped grant. Automatic HTTPS for hosted sites through Caddy's built-in ACME client, off by default per organization; instance TLS as self-signed, uploaded or Let's Encrypt. Git-backed projects connect through a GitHub App or GitLab OAuth, with an installation bound to one organization and forge addresses inside your network refused. Managed Postgres and MySQL engines with users, backups and shared ingress; TurboFabric overlay networks; datacenter networking with reserved ranges, routing policy and Docker address pools. Scheduled tasks from the console and from compose, rendered as systemd timers. Host metrics v6 across eight entity families. Every wire carries a version and a floor: a daemon below 0.1.0 keeps its connection but runs no commands until it updates; the app refuses an older instance and says which version it needs. Workers-only billing with a product-keyed tier ladder. The database schema is frozen at one baseline: every later migration is additive, the installer applies them with the instance's own migrate verb, and the instance refuses to serve a schema it does not ship.

title: Licensing
body: Control plane, daemon, UI, and contributor console stay AGPL-3.0-only. The UI adds an Apple App Store additional permission. The website is Apache-2.0 for code and CC BY 4.0 for documentation. Contributions use a CLA; trademarks stay separate from the software licenses.

title: Open-source launch packaging
body: Unified public naming, AGPL-3.0-only across repos, self-hosted documentation, and community routing via turbopanel/.github.
